implementation_notes: Diesel builds the query as a type-level AST: table methods (filter/select/order/limit) compose a SelectStatement whose QueryFragment the backend's QueryBuilder renders into SQL with bind parameters, and QueryId identifies the query's type so the prepared statement can be cached per shape. What replaces the classic query class is the type system plus the AST traits; because every conditional branch changes the type, dynamic shapes need into_boxed() - or the sea-query variant - so the static form stays justified exactly when the shape is known at compile time.
pitfalls: Every combinator changes the type: storing one query variable requires into_boxed() plus a matching Backend generic.
Bind data is collected when the statement is built, so rebuilding per call wastes the QueryId-keyed statement cache the crate provides.
The DSL is schema-checked at compile time, so a migration that renames a column breaks the build until the schema modules are regenerated.

variants.name: sea-query runtime AST builder (Query/Cond/Expr)
variants.implementation_notes: sea-query is the dynamic counterpart: Query::select().column(...).from(...).and_where(Expr::col("age").gte(...)) builds an enum AST that a backend builder (PostgresQueryBuilder, MysqlQueryBuilder, SqliteQueryBuilder) renders into (sql, Values) with the $N sequencing rewritten for you, apply_if covers optional filters and Cond::any/all express nested boolean trees. Choose it when the query shape is data-driven at runtime and Diesel's type-level composition would force boxing at every branch.
pitfalls: Columns are strings with no schema check, so a renamed column fails at runtime (or is caught only by the database).
Build with the same backend that executes: Values and placeholder sequencing are backend-specific.
An AST per request allocates; hoist fixed shapes or cache rendered SQL instead of rebuilding the whole tree each call.
